items.content:
Iraq says it lost $60b from Iran war, reaches understandings with US on Hormuz oil route
Iraqi oil will move through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said, under understandings reached with Washington.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein speaks during a joint press conference with Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed in Baghdad, Iraq, October 18, 2026.
Iraq has reached an understanding with the United States to allow Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera .
He said Iraq's losses from the Iran war and disruptions to oil exports had reached $60 billion.
Iraq's oil exports recovered in October after a sharp drop the previous month. Exports rose to about 3.5 million barrels per day from 2.65 million bpd in September, according to Iraqi energy officials.
Hussein also said the US Treasury had asked Iraq to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran , as part of Washington’s campaign to increase economic pressure on Tehran.
One of the two crossings that would remain open is in the Kurdistan Region .
Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, November 3, 2026 (credit: REUTERS/STRINGER)
Iraq has already closed some crossings with Iran in recent weeks, including the Al-Sheeb crossing in the south, citing the need for security and infrastructure upgrades. Tehran criticized that decision, saying Baghdad had not given advance notice.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while trying to traverse a route described as prohibited south of the key waterway, and that two other vessels had been seized.
A day later, the IRGC said two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to use unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sunday, Iran’s navy said an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Warren Buffett Has 1 Simple Rule for Surviving a Stock Market Crash, and History Says It's Never Once Failed - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Warren Buffett Has 1 Simple Rule for Surviving a Stock Market Crash, and History Says It's Never Once Failed  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Stocks have been struggling this week, and the Nasdaq officially entered a correction.
While it can be tempting to sell right now, Warren Buffett says otherwise.
The right strategy can protect your portfolio against even severe volatility.
It's been a roller-coaster of a week for the stock market. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +1.09% ) officially entered correction territory after falling by more than 10% from its October peak, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.31% ) and Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -0.46% ) are down by around 6% and 5%, respectively.
Investors are also grappling with the downturn. The Fear and Greed index measures investor sentiment based on multiple stock market metrics, and it quickly plunged into the "extreme fear" category amid this week's turbulence.
But it's not all bad news right now. Warren Buffett has some timeless advice for investing during crashes and bear markets, and history says this strategy has worked out every single time.
When the market is shaky, it can be tempting to avoid investing or even sell your stocks in fear that prices will fall further. According to Warren Buffett, though, that's one of the worst moves to make during a slump.
"A simple rule dictates my buying," Buffett explained in a 2008 opinion piece for The New York Times . "Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful." He went on to emphasize that "bad news is an investor's best friend. It lets you buy a slice of America's future at a marked-down price." In other words, when the future is bleak, buy more.
In the years following the publication of that piece, the S&P 500 soared by nearly 1,000%, and the investors who reaped the biggest rewards were those who stayed invested even when it was tough.
"Over the long term, the stock market news will be good," Buffett continued, noting the Dow's extraordinary rise from 66 to 11,497 during the 20th century.
"You might think it would have been impossible for an investor to lose money during a century marked by such an extraordinary gain. But some investors did. The hapless ones bought stocks only when they felt comfort in doing so and then proceeded to sell when the headlines made them queasy."
History says Buffett's strategy has never been wrong
No matter how severe the short-term volatility is, the market has always managed to recover.
During the dot-com bubble in 2000, for example, the S&P 500 fell by nearly 50% as the tech sector collapsed. It took until 2007 for the index to reach another all-time high, and just a few months later, the Great Recession began.
However, between 2000 and 2020, the S&P 500 still earned total returns of more than 224%. In other words, even if you'd invested at seemingly the worst moment -- immediately before the onset of two of the worst recessions in U.S. history -- you'd still have more than tripled your money over 20 years.
This trend holds up throughout history, too. Between 1919 and 2025, all of the S&P 500's rolling 20-year periods have ended in positive total returns, according to analysis from Crestmont Research. By holding an S&P 500 ETF or index fund for 20 years, it's historically been harder to lose money in the stock market than to make money.
Regardless of what's ahead for the market, continuing to invest is key. However, it's more important than ever to choose your stocks wisely. Weak companies can thrive during periods of economic prosperity, but recessions and bear markets will hit those stocks the hardest. The weakest of them may crash and never recover at all.
Companies with strong fundamentals -- such as a durable competitive advantage, healthy finances, and a competent leadership team -- are the most likely to rebound after a crash. The more of these stocks you own, the better prepared you'll be to not only survive a downturn, but thrive over time.

The S&P 500’s CAPE ratio was recently above 41, a level reached only once before (1999-2000).
Buffett’s rule to be fearful when others are greedy applies to “safe” dividend stocks too. Coca-Cola trades at a premium valuation after its 40% run over the past year.
Dividend investors can act on Buffett's advice by not paying any price for income, setting target prices for a shopping list, and turning dividends into dry powder.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.31% ) fell 4.4% on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025, while the Nasdaq slumped 5.5%. That deep sell-off pushed the Nasdaq into correction territory, with it tumbling more than 10% below its recent record.
Nobody knows whether that's the start of something bigger. But it landed in a market already priced for perfection. The S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio recently closed above 41, more than double its long-term average in the high teens. The only other time it has been this high was right before the dot-com bust.
I can't tell you exactly when the next crash might occur. However, the S&P 500 has experienced 13 bear markets (a decline of 20% or more) since 1929. They occur regularly, about every seven years on average, so another one is undoubtedly coming. While the last one was in 2022, that doesn't mean we won't experience another one sooner rather than later, given the currently elevated CAPE ratio. With another crash inevitable, Warren Buffett's most famous advice is the best guide I know for preparing for one. For dividend investors, it boils down to three specific moves.
Buffett's rule: be fearful when others are greedy
Buffett's best-known investing rule is: "Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful." He wrote it down in his 1986 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders.
Buffett's rule isn't to try to predict a crash; it's to become more disciplined when the market becomes overly optimistic. A CAPE ratio above 40 suggests that optimism is ruling the day.
Here's the part dividend investors won't want to miss. Greed isn't limited to AI stocks. It shows up in "safe" dividend payers, too. Coca-Cola ( KO -0.06% ) , one of Buffett's best-known holdings, has surged 40% over the past year. That puts it at a very rich valuation , trading at nearly 29 times earnings, well above the S&P 500's 23.5 times earnings. While Coca-Cola is a premium company, that's still very expensive.

Here are three practical ways dividend investors can heed Buffett's rule of being fearful when others are greedy, so that you can be greedy when others are fearful.
Stop paying any price for income. The surge in Coca-Cola's stock price has driven its dividend yield down from 3% to 2.2% over the past year. As a result, an investment today would generate far less dividend income than one made when the yield was higher. The tip is to compare a potential dividend stock investment's current yield with its own history. If it's far below, stop adding. You don't need to sell great businesses, but you also don't need to buy more shares at high valuations either.
Put together a shopping list with target prices. Pick five to eight high-quality dividend payers you'd love to own cheaper, then turn the yield you want into a target price by dividing the annual dividend by your desired yield. For example, Coca-Cola pays $2.12 a share a year. If you'd love to buy Coke at a 3% yield, you'd target a purchase around $71, about 25% below where the stock recently traded (around $96). If the market gets fearful and Coca-Cola falls to your target price, that's the time to get greedy.
Turn your dividends into dry powder. With valuations elevated across the market, it's time to consider pausing your automatic dividend reinvestment program, at least for stocks trading at stretched valuations. Let those payouts pile up in cash, allowing you to build buying power without selling a single share. Berkshire does this on a larger scale: it ended the second quarter with $364.7 billion in cash, giving it significant buying power.
The proof: What happens to dividend stocks when the market crashes
Dividend stocks tend to be more resilient investments. We've seen that during prior stock market crashes. For example, when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the S&P 500 experienced a 47% crash over the next two years. High-quality dividend stocks, on the other hand, delivered much better performance. S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats® (the term Dividend Aristocrats® is a registered trademark of Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC) gained 4.7% during that period, outperforming the market by a whopping 51.4%. Dividend Aristocrats® also outperformed the S&P 500 during the global financial crisis (-55% to -47.2%). However, they don't always outperform during bear markets (-1.4% underperformance during the COVID crash of 2020).
The lesson is that while dividend stocks typically hold up well during a crash, that's not always the case. It's why investors should avoid buying dividend stocks at premium prices in today's market.
Just because another crash is inevitable isn't a reason not to dump your best dividend stocks. The goal isn't to guess the top; it's to be ready when prices change.
Start building cash by holding off on new purchases at stretched valuations (including dividend reinvestment) and put together your watch list, so you're ready for the next crash. The key to following Buffett's advice is to be disciplined now so that you can view a future crash not as a time to be fearful but as a time to get greedy.

items.title: Why Apple’s M6 Chip Can’t Hold Its Own Against Any NVIDIA GPU - Engadget
items.summary: Why Apple’s M6 Chip Can’t Hold Its Own Against Any NVIDIA GPU  Engadget
items.content:
Why Apple’s M6 Chip Can’t Hold Its Own Against Any NVIDIA GPU
Apple has just announced the arrival of its M6 chip, but it still can't compete with NVIDIA
In introducing the latest Mac mini , Apple also debuted its sixth generation of M-series processors for Macs. Apple of course extols the M6 chip as extremely powerful, providing significant boosts to CPU and performance, and there's at least a little merit to those claims. In our review testing, the machine didn't miss a beat in everything from photo editing to 4K video transcoding.
If you're not wedded to the Apple ecosystem, it's important to weigh the M6's processor tech against what's available on the PC side of the fence. And if you're serious about graphics, that probably means computers with a dedicated NVIDIA GPU. In fact, you'll want  a dedicated GPU for meaningful performance on most PCs since integrated graphics chips tend to be good for little more than streaming and light gaming.
In short, most NVIDIA GPUs are going to wipe the floor with the M6 when it comes to gaming and other real-time graphics tasks. That said, if you're willing to lock into the Apple ecosystem, the M6 can potentially deliver what you need while costing a lot less.
It's a bit difficult to offer an apples-to-apples comparison, if you'll forgive the joke. Whereas the M6 is an all-in-one processor with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores, the performance of NVIDIA GPUs is dependent not just on the card you pick but the AMD or Intel CPU you pair it with. Moreover, the best way of benchmarking Mac graphics is often through Metal scores, and Windows PCs can't run software using the Apple-optimized Metal API. They veer toward DirectX 12 or Vulkan instead.
Thankfully, there is a roundabout way of tackling the question.  MacRumors notes that the Geekbench OpenCL score for the new Mini's other processor option, the M5 Ultra, is roughly in line with NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 4080. The M5 Ultra also has a 366,744 Metal score. By contrast, the M6 has a Metal score of 93,217, nearly four times less.
That's bad because the RTX 4080 represents last-generation NVIDIA architecture from 2022. You can already push the limits of RTX 50-series GPUs in some games (speaking from personal experience), and since real-time 3D graphics are continually evolving, it's doubtful the M6 will be able to keep pace at all by 2028 when the RTX 60-series cards are rumored to come out.
A quick reality check, however — if you're not obsessed with maximum detail or futureproofing, the M6 does fine. We found the M6 Mini averages 55 frames per second in Cyberpunk 2077 with default Mac quality settings, which is plenty smooth, and many games aren't as demanding. For tasks that don't involve real-time rendering, like video transcoding, any gap with a comparable NVIDIA-based PC should be minor to non-existent. Most people probably don't care if a video exports a few seconds faster.
The M6 wins in one major aspect, and that's cost. Although the new Mini's $900 sticker price is a $300 hike over the previous generation, even an RTX 5060 is going to cost you north of $450, and that's before you pair it with the other components needed to build a working PC. Meanwhile, high-end RTX 5080 cards are going for over $2,000, which is enough to buy a MacBook Pro.
Viewed in that light, it may easily be worth putting up with Apple's less impressive performance. You could buy an M6 Mini today, then the inevitable follow-up two years later, and still save money versus buying some NVIDIA-powered gaming laptops. (The Mini doesn't ship with a display or input devices, mind you.)
One problem with all Macs is compatibility. While there's no shortage of productivity apps for macOS, most games are PC-first not just because of an existing customer base, but also that greater amount of horsepower. If I were to choose a computer primarily for gaming, I'd rather buy Valve's $1,050 Steam Machine , which can run most modern games with console-like simplicity despite being based on custom AMD hardware.

Nvidia launches investigation after CEO Jensen Huang admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, "I was unfaithful to my wife," according to The New York Times .
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy (Getty)
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of "groundless smears and slanders" against the Asian country.
Nvidia's board "prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," Sunday's company press release read.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."
Nvidia announced Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation 'in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort' (Getty)
CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said. There was no word of Huang's position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team."
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption."
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn't unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, "I just can't comment because of the nature of it."
Late last month, it was reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center who U.S. officials suspect was feeding information to Beijing (AFP/Getty)
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for "Super Intelligence" and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.
"We're leading China in AI," the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . "We're the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

Markets Are Pricing in a Fed Rate Hike in December. Here's What Investors Should Do, According to History.
Kevin Warsh has already presided over one Federal Reserve rate hike during his first few months as Fed chair. And now another rate increase could be on the way.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted to leave the federal funds rate unchanged at its October meeting. However, CME Group 's (NASDAQ: CME) FedWatch projects an 81.2% probability of a rate hike at the committee's December 2026 meeting.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
This likelihood of a second rate increase raises a key question for investors: What should I do? History has four good answers to that question.
Image source: Getty Images. 1. Don't blindly sell stocks
Investors could be tempted to run for the hills and sell all or most of their stocks. History shows that's a really bad move.
The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has risen by an average of around 9% over the 12 months following a new rate-hike cycle, according to research conducted by Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS). Granted, the index initially declined by roughly 2% on average during the first three months after the first rate increase of a cycle. But selling stocks en masse early in a rate-hike cycle would have usually cost investors in the past.
Some stocks outperform others in environments with rising interest rates. History shows that focusing on the most promising sectors can pay off.
For example, energy stocks were the clear winner during the Fed's last major series of rate hikes from March 2022 through July 2023. The State Street Energy Select SPDR ETF (NYSEMKT: XLE), which owns shares of 21 energy sector leaders, jumped around 18% during the period. Oil and gas giant ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) and pipeline stock Energy Transfer LP (TXSE: ET) delivered even higher returns.
For investors who own bonds, shifting from long-duration to short-duration bonds is practically a no-brainer. When interest rates rise, bond prices tend to fall. Longer-duration bonds get hit the hardest. The good news is that you can buy a short-term U.S. Treasury bond that's essentially risk-free and get a yield north of 4% right now.
As important as the FOMC vote in December is, it's even more important for investors to read between the lines with the Fed's actions. The trick to doing this is to analyze the updated dot-plot projection, a chart that shows how individual FOMC participants expect short-term interest rates to move.
In particular, pay attention to how aggressively policymakers expect rates to increase. Goldman Sachs' research found that especially rapid rate hikes have led to worse stock market performance in the past.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again
In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $2,426,128 today.*
Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo
The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo .
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize , which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild .
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war.
“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell,” he said.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely” if negotiations progress over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said when asked about continued US strikes on Iran during a phone interview reported by CNN. “I would [continue], if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” he added.
Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He also said that the US has 38 bridges in Iran’s crosshairs that US forces “can knock down in literally one hour”.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry also quoted Araghchi in an earlier statement on Sunday that said Iran would “not go easy on American targets” in the region.
Araghchi’s statements came after reports by state media that an oil tanker caught fire earlier that morning after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz , citing Iran’s navy.
The navy claimed the ship’s identification systems were turned off and it was travelling in the no-go zone of the strait.
An adviser to Iran’s commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said that weapons have been “secured for years to come”.
“The armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe,” warned IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali in a statement on Telegram.
“As senior commanders of the armed forces have pointed out, we have upgraded our capabilities in the post-Ramadan War period,” Belali said.
The back-and-fourth between Iranian and US leaders comes following US midterm elections in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, soundly defeating Trump’s Republican Party.
Araghchi alleged that negotiations have been delayed as a result of the elections, but he awaits the path forward, Iranian state media reported.
“It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits,” the foreign minister said. “We have to wait.”

items.title: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war - The Guardian
items.summary: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war  The Guardian
items.content:
Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war
In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities
For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.
If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.
Two Flamingo missiles had slammed into a pair of buildings, including a facility known as 106A, a “clean room” where motherboards for the Soyuz launch systems were assembled.
Satellite imagery shows damage, including a hole in a roof, at the Soyuz production facility in Samara after Ukrainian strikes in August. Photograph: Vantor In the midst of other Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries and industry, the Samara attack stood out, providing evidence of a spreading war, the geographical impact of which – already felt across Europe via hybrid attacks, and assaults on civilian shipping in the Black Sea – has crept into the domain of space.
In a conflict that is redefining warfare through the heavy use of drones and battlefield sensors, access to space and the satellites that power those systems – as well as the ability to disrupt enemy operations there – has become ever more critical.
The attack on Samara was a case in point, hitting the rockets that deliver Russia’s new Rassvet satellite system, which is being rapidly deployed as a replacement for Elon Musk’s Starlink, from which Russia was shut out earlier this year.
In addition, Ukraine has attacked other sites belonging to Roscosmos this year, including Korolyov, a large complex north of Moscow, and a Ukrainian-built radio telescope captured by Russia in Crimea.
Russia’s attempts to rapidly deploy its Rassvet network are not the only challenge from space that Ukraine faces. Moscow has also used Oreshnik ballistic missiles on at least three occasions – a system that launches into near space, then deploys multiple independently targetable warheads initially designed for nuclear weapons.
All of this has prompted Kyiv to intensify efforts to diversify its own access to space-based systems away from the US and Starlink, which was controversially choked in recent weeks, and to develop new space countermeasures against threats such as the Oreshnik.
Ukraine has conducted at least three tests of near-space interceptions as it has sought to launch its own sovereign satellites, joining a rapidly expanding number of countries working towards a foothold in space.
That became a reality last month when Ukraine and Denmark’s GomSpace announced they had successfully launched the Obria Nano, the first test satellite for a future independent Ukrainian communications network, reportedly envisaging about 245 satellites.
An illustration of the Obria Nano in orbit. Photograph: GomSpace Group AB ‘Everyone wants their own version of Starlink’
The increasing incursion of the Ukraine conflict into space, say experts, is only the latest evidence of the rapid militarisation of a domain the treaties for which remain ill defined, outdated and difficult to enforce.
In September the US air force secretary, Troy Meink, admitted for the first time that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” amid reports that Russia had regularly flown its satellites close to US and other countries’ assets in space.
As if to underline that point, a few weeks later a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, was observed aggressively manoeuvring towards a commercial radar satellite operated by the Finnish group Iceye that provides three-dimensional terrain imaging to the Ukrainian military, in what experts described as an act of deliberate harassment.
“[Space warfare] has been talked about as the future,” says Dr Elena Grossfeld, an expert on space and security at the Swedish Defence University. “But we’re already in that future.”
For Russia, she argues, space has become essential to military success, with Moscow treating offensive operations there as a precursor to broader conflict in a new reality where war is inseparable from satellite-based intelligence and targeting.
“This started before the war in Ukraine,” she said. “The US Space Force [then second in command, Gen David Thompson] said in 2021 that the US was seeing daily attacks [by Russia and China] on US satellites.
“They are not necessarily kinetic [attacks], but now with the war and with everyone’s dependency on space for intelligence and communications, it has become front and centre.”
While Grossfeld said Russia’s intention in the recent “bullying” of the Iceye satellite was not clear, one possibility was to force it to use fuel to change course and in doing so shorten its lifespan.
That is not the only tactic that has been seen. Russia has also used signal jamming, laser-dazzling of satellites, and placed “inspector” spy satellites near foreign space assets.
A Soyuz-2.1b carrier rocket with a military satellite blasts off from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region. Photograph: AP Complicating what is happening in space, experts say, is that treaties on governance in space, and deployment of weapons, have in recent years been overtaken.
Victoria Samson, the head of the space security and stability programme at the Secure World Foundation, which advocates for space safety and sustainability, noted a rapid increase in the number of countries operating in space, in tandem with the expansion of commercial activities by companies such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin.
But while many countries have opted to use SpaceX for its satellite launches, Musk’s recent actions towards Ukraine, cutting Starlink data speeds, have forced a rapid rethink of whether to rely on unreliable and sometimes ideologically led commercial ventures.
“The big shift in the past decade,” said Samson, “has been towards commercial space operations and that has been an issue in the current conflict [in Ukraine].”
Like Grossfeld, Samson sees frictions in space becoming more overt. “It’s all part of strategic competition,” she said, describing the recent Russian satellite-bullying incident. She added that with more escalation, there had been “more openness on the US side to talk about what they are doing [in relation to weapons in space] while Russia and China are working on a lot of the same stuff.
“Then there is the issue of space being used in an active military conflict. We have already seen Russia jamming GPS, which has resulted in aviation being disrupted over the Baltics. But it has been particularly visible in the issue of Starlink and in pauses by the US to sharing satellite intelligence with Ukraine [that warns] of incoming ballistic missiles.”
If there has been a consequence of Musk’s and the Trump administration’s unreliability, Samson believes, it has been to push countries to seek alternatives. “Like the Russians with [the] Rassvet network, everyone now wants their own versions of Starlink, including the Europeans.”
For Ukraine, said Fedir Venislavskyi, the head of the state security subcommittee of its parliamentary defence committee, that meant a “sovereign” Ukrainian presence in space, now achieved via the Obria Nano satellite.
“Since the war the space domain has been crucial for Ukrainian forces and that has been underlined by recent events – whether at the instigation of the US government or from SpaceX – where we saw communications drop and jeopardise our military’s command-and-control systems.
“Now we need to raise it to another level, not least because the enemy is already threatening Ukrainian territory from international space via Oreshnik missiles. It’s essential we’re not shortsighted about this risk.”
With Russian launch sites now beyond the range of Ukraine’s longest-range missiles, Ukraine has instead conducted three tests on exo-atmospheric kill systems to intercept launches in near space, including launches of weapons piggybacked on very high-flying aircraft.
“It is a priority,” said Venislavskyi. “We’ve already demonstrated launches of exo-atmospheric systems and we are working to see if we can get that in production.” However, he admitted, given the huge demands of the war, funding would be a significant issue.

items.title: China heads towards high income status and policy reckoning at home and abroad - East Asia Forum
items.summary: China heads towards high income status and policy reckoning at home and abroad  East Asia Forum
items.content:
China heads towards high income status and policy reckoning at home and abroad
Even as China's approaches high-income status, its investment-led growth model continues to generate excessive savings, weak household consumption and large external surpluses that increasingly provoke trade restrictions abroad. Beijing’s efforts to stimulate consumption through subsidies and cheaper credit are unlikely to overcome deeper structural problems, including income inequality, inadequate social protection and restrictions on migrants’ access to public services. The concentration of political authority, and the uncertainty surrounding leadership succession, risk reinforcing policy inertia, making reforms to both economic institutions and political leadership essential to sustaining China’s growth and managing its global economic impact.
China is on course to become a high-income economy in 2027. By World Bank standards, its gross national income per capita is now just US$145 short of the high-income threshold . But achieving and sustaining this status will require Beijing to strengthen consumption-driven growth and address institutionalised policy inertia.
Market opening and large-scale reform have channelled high savings rates towards investment, propelling China’s unprecedented growth. The scale of the Chinese economy gives it enormous forward momentum, but also makes its growth engine difficult to turn or stop.
China’s national saving rate was 42.7 per cent of GDP in 2024, while household consumption has languished below 40 per cent since 2005. Savings that domestic investment cannot absorb spill over into the current account surplus, which reached a record US$735 billion in 2025, or 3.7 per cent of GDP. This is up from US$353 billion in 2007, though that figure then represented a record 9.8 per cent of GDP.
China’s scale transforms domestic imbalances into international externalities, generating political reactions, trade restrictions and economic security responses that constrain its policy choices further. This is something of a reverse exorbitant privilege — while the United States derives exceptional advantages from its central position in the international monetary system, China incurs exceptional costs from its importance in the economic system. Its size magnifies both the global consequences of its policies and the international reaction to them.
A domestic imbalance would go unnoticed in a smaller economy, but the scale of China’s imbalance puts pressure on other countries’ industries. Trading partners respond with restrictions that narrow Beijing’s policy options, prolonging the very overcapacity they target. US tariffs and EU trade restrictions on China are symptoms, not the root cause, which lies in uneven underlying saving and consumption structures.
Beijing has rolled out a range of new consumption policies in its 2026 15th Five-Year Plan, from trade-in subsidies to nationwide childcare support. But these measures are limited in their scale and overall effectiveness.
In the first of this week’s lead articles , Yixiao Zhou examines Beijing’s expansion of interest subsidies on consumer loans in August 2026. As Zhou points out, subsidised credit which lowers the price of borrowing does little when the fundamental problem is one of low consumer confidence.
Uncertainty about future income prospects have caused household loans to shrink by a record 650.7 billion RMB (US$93.7 billion) in February 2026 through early mortgage repayments and larger down payments. Households repairing their balance sheets are unlikely to increase spending for a 1 percentage point interest subsidy. Those who do respond will already be the most creditworthy, and would have spent anyway. The aggregate figures also conceal a K-shaped divergence , in which key sectors of the economy travel in different directions that credit subsidies cannot reach.
How policy inertia plays out in China will importantly depend on who is in control.
The 21st Party Congress in 2027 will see a leadership reshuffle among China’s top policymakers, which will shape the economic agenda just as much as any planning document. Even if President Xi begins a fourth term, as is expected, five of the six other Politburo Standing Committee members will have reached the conventional retirement age of 68, including Premier Li Qiang and Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi.
In our second lead article this week , Xiangyu Ma treats the appointment of 21 provincial Party leaders since April 2026 as a window through which to assess the possible character of the next Politburo. He sets out three possible scenarios: a high-turnover overhaul of the policy leadership; a low-turnover reshuffle that deepens Xi’s personalist rule; and selective continuity with exemptions for a few of Xi’s closest allies.
A key question, Ma reckons, is whether Beijing can keep continuity at the top while opening a path upward for the next generation. The post-1960s cohort has waited longer to enter the country’s top offices than its predecessors. Xi entered the Standing Committee at 54, while today’s youngest member, Ding Xuexiang, joined at 60.
Regular turnover, Ma argues, moderates younger cadres’ career expectations and rewards performance. When openings shrink and the rules grow less predictable, competition shifts from delivering results to factional infighting. Then those with little prospects of promotion lie low and do little.
The inertia within China’s growth model and the choices made by its top leadership stem from the same root issue of concentration. Beijing has concentrated resources in investment rather than households to drive growth, and income inequality has widened as a result. In 2025, the median urban disposable income was about two-and-a-half-times rural disposable incomes.
Unequal pension coverage and the hukou system, which restricts internal migrants’ access to urban public services, give the least protected households the strongest reasons to save as a precaution. Zhou estimates that granting urban hukou status to migrant workers could lift their consumption by nearly 30 per cent. The 15th Five-Year Plan has made ‘investing in people’ a priority, but how fiscal policy will support it remains to be seen.
Decision-making authority has also remained in a small circle rather than a broad bench of successors under Xi, to keep policy and implementation unified. The new cohort of provincial chiefs have built their careers on promoting investment and output rather than social protection and a national leadership selected from their ranks will have passed a loyalty test to Xi. This does not suggest a constituency focused on consumption transition.
There are signs that Beijing acknowledges the need to change direction. Proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan call for a ‘significant rise’ in the household consumption rate and commits to providing basic public services by place of residence. And Beijing’s 2024 leadership development plan calls for Party officials to move down as well as up and for the routine selection of younger cadres .
At the end of 2012, Xi said that reform ‘ is always in progress and never complete ’. The inertia now afflicting policy flexibility are legacies of China’s earlier successful reforms. The cost of delay is already visible.
Beijing has the resources to adjust its domestic imbalances and carry out its leadership renewal. It must now apply Xi’s principle — that ‘problems arising in reform can only be solved through reform’ — and keep both reforms moving.

items.title: Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections
items.summary: France says European officials will attend this week's U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the first three-way round of negotiations since February.
items.content:
Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections France says European officials will attend this week's U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, the first three-way round of negotiations since February.
Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections
A view through the destroyed walls of a kindergarten shows a large bomb crater and a damaged residential apartment building following a missile attack in Kyiv, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026.
European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.
"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.
Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, right, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference in Berlin, Germany, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.
Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.
Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.
For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.
For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.
This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.
The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, interacts with people at the monument to merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky, leaders of the struggle against foreign invaders in 1612, in Red Square in Moscow, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, during National Unity Day celebrations.
Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.
Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

items.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
items.summary: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
items.content:
Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
Image caption, Uninjured passengers and bystanders searched derailed carriages for injured people
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.
Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.
Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.
Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

items.title: AMD or Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy With $1,000 Today? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: AMD or Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Would I Buy With $1,000 Today?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
AMD's fiscal Q3 results were good, but its data center segment growth did slow.
Nvidia's fiscal Q3 results are still to come, but it has a track record of outperforming AMD.
AMD ( AMD +11.04% ) and Nvidia ( NVDA +2.77% ) are two of the largest competitors in the AI processor industry. The third primary one is Broadcom ( AVGO +0.74% ) , but its niche in that segment differs from theirs. Nvidia and AMD compete in the same field, designing powerful general-purpose chips while Broadcom designs highly specialized computing units for specific AI workloads.
AMD's share price has more than doubled so far this year, seriously outperforming Nvidia, which is just about flat. However, what matters more for investors is what's ahead. So, if you've got $1,000 ready to invest, is AMD or Nvidia the better stock to buy today? I think it's clearly Nvidia, and the numbers speak for themselves.
Investors are still waiting for Nvidia's fiscal Q3 results
On Nov. 3, AMD reported its fiscal Q3 earnings. Nvidia's fiscal quarters end one month later than AMD's, so we'll have to wait until Nov. 17 to hear from Nvidia. However, AMD's results were pretty strong.
What investors care about most when comparing these two are their data center divisions. For AMD, this segment saw revenue growth of 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. While that was a strong result, it was still a slowdown from Q2's 107% growth to $6.7 billion.

When Nvidia reports on Nov. 17, investors will be looking closely to see if it follows suit with a growth slowdown, or if it continues to report accelerating revenue gains. During Nvidia's fiscal Q2, its data center revenue rose 117% year over year to $89 billion. So, despite sales that were more than 10 times larger than AMD's, it was growing significantly faster. If it can keep up the trend of growing faster than AMD, I think this scores a major point in Nvidia's favor, as it's far harder for such a massive business to grow that fast.
However, Nvidia's overall business is far more leveraged to the state of the data center segment than AMD is. In fiscal Q2, Nvidia's total revenue was $96.2 billion, so its $89 billion data center revenue made up over 90% of its total. In Q3, AMD's $8.5 billion total was well over half of AMD's $13.3 billion, but its other segments make a much more meaningful contribution to its results. This could be a bad thing for AMD if data center spending takes off over the next few years (like it's projected to do), or it could be a good thing if the data center build-out slows due to new laws and regulations being passed.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $4.50T
Regardless, Nvidia still has the growth edge here, but it also holds another huge advantage.
In 2026, AMD and Nvidia's businesses have done quite well and are delivering similar levels of growth. However, AMD's stock has soared while Nvidia's has stagnated. While I'm not sure why there is a performance split between these two, it has revealed some pricing discrepancies in the stocks.
As we get closer to turning the calendar to 2027, I think valuing the stocks based on next year's earnings estimates is a smart idea. AMD trades at 30 times next year's expected earnings, which is a bit expensive. However, Nvidia trades at just under 13 times next year's earnings, which is an absolute bargain price.
So, AMD is far more expensive than Nvidia, and I think that's the final piece in the puzzle here. It's not often you can buy shares of a company that is by far the largest name in its industry and also growing faster than its top competitor at a huge discount to the competition, but that's exactly what's going on with Nvidia's stock.
As a result, I think that Nvidia is the best semiconductor stock to invest $1,000 in right now. AMD has had a strong run this year, but now it's about time for the leader to reassert itself. I think Nvidia's 2027 stock performance could mirror AMD's performance in 2026, and if I'm right, its shareholders will be well rewarded.

items.content:
Lisa Nandy said on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that an ‘honest conversation’ was needed after a decade in which Britons had been badly let down. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA
Lisa Nandy said on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that an ‘honest conversation’ was needed after a decade in which Britons had been badly let down. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA
Lisa Nandy wary of ‘circular arguments’ about rejoining EU
Culture secretary pushes back against talk of revisiting Brexit but says closer ties would fulfil referendum promises
One of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said she wants to avoid “circular arguments” about whether the UK should rejoin the EU, underlining divisions at the top of government over revisiting Brexit .
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, appeared to suggest she was not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc, but she said the prime minister should still pursue closer ties to fulfil the promises made at the time of the referendum.
She is one of a handful of cabinet ministers who are concerned about Burnham’s plan for an “honest conversation” with the public about Brexit and who are privately warning it could reopen a row that would only benefit Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
“I do not believe that anybody wants to repeat circular arguments about in or out, leave or remain. I do think, though, that over the last decade we have let the British people down very badly,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.
Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit
Nandy, whose Wigan seat voted overwhelmingly for leave in 2016, and who is one of the most cautious in the cabinet about reversing Brexit, was asked if she wanted to go back in. “I don’t know if that’s a choice we have,” she said.
However, she did concede that Burnham was trying to address the failings of the Brexit deal, telling Sky News it was important to “be honest” and highlight that “the deal that we got is not what we were promised”.
The culture secretary stressed there were “trade-offs and choices” to be made which involved a conversation with people across the country, indicating that Brexit would be a key theme of the next election campaign.
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday. Downing Street sources said he would use it to get Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.
In private, EU counterparts will be expecting Burnham to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to move beyond Labour’s “red lines” on the bloc after the next election.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and youth experience visas are expected to be confirmed.
Burnham said at the weekend there was more to come. “This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition,” he told the Sunday Mirror.
Officials will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) Safe defence fund , collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and visas for touring artists.
Soon after the Brussels summit, Burnham is expected to give a speech setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU, arguing it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. No 10 sources said he wanted to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion.
Senior government figures say Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be solely confirmatory.
“You can’t ask people to vote on an undefined plan like in 2016. That was David Cameron’s mistake,” one said.
However, Burnham has faced reservations from others within his cabinet. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, are cautious about pushing to fully rejoin.
The EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said London could not have the “single market à la carte” by cherrypicking which of the four freedoms – including freedom of movement – it would like in future negotiations.
“There is no cherrypicking. There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other,” he told the BBC.
Nandy was forced to reject allegations that celebrating the UK rejoining the Erasmus plus scheme by linking it to Remembrance Sunday was inappropriate, after suggesting it would help to honour “the immense courage of those who served our country” before Remembrance Sunday.
Kevin Hollinrake, the Tory chair, suggested she was using the national civic occasion to “try to make an EU membership pitch”. He said: “Our veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme.”
Speaking on Sky News, Nandy responded: “They are the only party that is talking about Brexit and the EU. What we are announcing this weekend is that we’re going to widen the Erasmus scheme.
“I cannot see what is political about saying that we want young people from every part of this country to understand the contribution that their grandparents and great-grandparents made, not just to us but to many, many lives of people that they had never met,” she added.

items.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Faces Pressure Over China Chip Deals, Alleged Romance  Seoul Economic Daily
items.content:
Note: Global Morning Briefing summarizes global news as reported by Seoul Economic Daily (Seoul Economic Daily).
From NewMatrix to MegaSpeed: Nvidia's China Deals Under Scrutiny
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. EPA/Yonhap Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang faces mounting political pressure after Democrats captured both chambers of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections. Suspicions that export reviews of artificial intelligence chips bound for China were lax have been compounded by reports that he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.
The New York Times reported on the 7th that NewMatrix, a Chinese company cleared by the U.S. Commerce Department to handle Nvidia's H200 chips, appears to have little substance. Despite holding a license, the company showed almost no trace of business activity, and its registered address was an empty space, the paper said. Its owners are also linked to Wise Road Capital, a private equity firm placed on an export control list in 2024, raising the possibility that the company is a front. In September, MagInfra, another Chinese firm licensed to handle H200 chips, also drew suspicion of being a shell company.
Unlike the administration of Joe Biden, which expanded semiconductor export restrictions, President Donald Trump approved H200 sales to China last December after repeated lobbying by Huang.
According to the Financial Times, the U.S. government prepared an internal memo stating that Huang had been in a relationship with Alice Huang. Alice Huang, an executive at MegaSpeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, is under investigation over allegations that she sought to collect information on Nvidia's technology and U.S. policy toward China. MegaSpeed is suspected of having purchased more than 136,000 graphics processing units since 2023 and leasing computing power to companies including Alibaba.
Bloomberg projected that the Democratic-led Congress taking office in January will use its investigative and subpoena powers to examine whether Nvidia has complied with export controls. Legislation such as the AI Overwatch Act, which would restrict AI chip exports to countries of concern including China, could also gain momentum.
Data Center Ownership Shifts in U.S., With Moderates Holding the Key
A sign supporting a ban on data center construction stands in front of a home near Meta's Prometheus data center campus in New Albany, Ohio, on Nov. 1, local time, ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. AFP/Yonhap
After Democrats pushed into Republican strongholds in the midterm elections, the share of data center power capacity under construction in states with Democratic governors jumped to 60.3% from 25.0%. Democrats, who have criticized data center policy, now must take responsibility for it themselves.
An analysis of Compute Atlas data by Seoul Economic Daily found that Democrats won Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa to take 28 states, compared with 20 for Republicans, and that power capacity under construction in those states totaled 77.4 gigawatts. Facilities in operation, under construction or planned also numbered 1,918 in Democratic states, or 66.4%, more than double the 939 facilities, or 32.5%, in Republican states.
Even so, a complete halt to construction is seen as unlikely. ING estimated that technology investment accounted for about one-third of U.S. growth this year, and Bloomberg reported that China's energy investment tied to AI infrastructure reached $940 billion, the largest in the world. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat, called a construction halt "idiocy" in March. A draft paper cited by The Washington Post found that data centers accounted for only 4% of the increase in electricity bills from 2020 to 2025.
Moderates also hold the upper hand within the party. Only eight winners in the House and one in the Senate came from the democratic socialist wing. Governor Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania attracted large-scale investments including $20 billion from Amazon, and party leaders such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate leader Chuck Schumer have leaned toward accepting investment with conditions. United States-based chipmaker Nvidia is investigating its chief executive officer, billionaire Jensen Huang, after he confirmed he had an intimate relationship with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence.
In an announcement on Sunday, Nvidia said the probe would be conducted by a “committee of independent directors” with outside counsel.

“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia’s board of directors said.
It said the board continued to have “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team”. Huang will continue to lead Nvidia during the probe.
The investigation follows a report in The New York Times last month that Jensen may have been the target of a Chinese espionage plot.
China and the US have been in competition to dominate key tech sectors like artificial intelligence (AI).
Amid the AI boom, Nvidia has seen demand for its chips and programming interfaces explode, resulting in the company being valued in the trillions of dollars.
For years, the US has sought to restrict the export of advanced chips to China, fearing the Asian superpower could gain an edge over its technology and military sectors.
But on October 29, The New York Times said it had obtained exclusive information that a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le, sought to cultivate close ties with Jensen Huang in an effort to glean information about Nvidia’s technology.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, has denied any allegations of spying in the case.
The New York Times also reported that Alice Huang’s employer, Megaspeed, had become one of Nvidia’s largest buyers, purchasing some $4.8bn in equipment from the US firm.
Jensen Huang’s ties to Alice Huang, who is of no relation, spurred fierce bipartisan backlash in the US Congress in the aftermath of the report.
“For months, bipartisan members of Congress have raised concerns about NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips going to China,” Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote in a statement.
“NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers. And we need to pass bipartisan legislation we have ready to stop advanced American technology from going to China.”
Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives also called on Huang to appear and testify before Congress about the affair on November 18.
“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” Republicans John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford said in a statement.
In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang had admitted to having an extramarital relationship.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse ‌for what I did,” Huang said.
Nvidia has grown rapidly in recent years with the rise of AI, producing chips for large language models developed by companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google.
Huang has also been closely working with US President Donald Trump since the Republican leader returned to office in 2025.
In August of that year, the Trump administration announced it would take a 15 percent cut of certain Nvidia chip sales to China.
Trump reportedly bought as much as $1.6m in Nvidia stock and sold about $1m in August, ahead of November’s midterm elections.
After the midterm races last Tuesday, stocks for AI-related companies, including Nvidia, tumbled in reaction to widespread Republican losses.
Trump has pushed back against calls to regulate AI companies, but many Democrats during the midterms campaigned on placing restrictions on the companies, including on the construction of data centres.
Nvidia lost $450bn in market value in a single trading day last week, but it rebounded on Friday, regaining 4 percent of its losses.

TSMC began drafting plans to produce a particular type of advanced memory chips, known as 3D DRAM, at the request of Nvidia Corp, its biggest customer, The Information reported, citing two people familiar with the plans.
The company is also exploring acquiring a plant and converting it for memory production, the report said.

The push is helmed by Hsu Kuo-chin (徐國晉), a vice president who oversees advanced packaging at TSMC, it said.

While TSMC did not address memory chips specifically, the company said its mission is to be “the trusted technology and capacity provider” of logic chips, which process data as opposed to storing it.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
