Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
There's one question on everybody's mind entering the new trading week: Where are artificial intelligence stocks going next? The engine of the four-year-old bull market is coming off a bruising week , sparked by the midterm elections, when gubernatorial candidates who support restrictions on data center development won big in states like Texas and Ohio. Voters across the country also approved local ballot measures that could slow the pace of AI investment and construction. As Jim Cramer made clear at Friday's Annual Meeting , this is a real risk to the future earnings of chipmakers, electrical equipment suppliers and other companies with brimming order books to support the AI buildout. We take it seriously and may need to make further adjustments to our stock portfolio to reduce AI exposure. This headwind didn't blow in from nowhere. It's why we exited Corning in early September and Broadcom in late October , and two months ago initiated positions in the non-tech stocks of Kimberly-Clark and Bank of New York . The upshot after such a whirlwind week for the market? No Club holdings are reporting in the coming days and the economic calendar is also fairly light. Here's a closer look at what to expect: 1. AI earnings: Neocloud CoreWeave's earnings report on Tuesday night will help determine whether the AI trade can regain momentum. Even before the election, we've been paying close attention to CoreWeave's bonds and stock as a barometer for souring investor appetite for AI names. How the market responds to CoreWeave's results and commentary on the conference call could have far-reaching implications. "That's going to be the one," Jim said at the Annual Meeting. "You either believe [CEO Michael Intrator] and you see the stock go up and you realize that the AI trade is on. Or you don't believe Michael and the stock plummets, and it'll be a really bad day. ... CoreWeave is so important. It's insanely important." On Thursday morning, CoreWeave's peer in the neocloud game, Nebius , delivers earnings of its own. And that evening, networking giant Cisco Systems and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials will release quarterly results. Both companies are also cogs in the AI trade, so they're firmly on our radar alongside CoreWeave and Nebius. 2. Inflation and Fed speakers: Inflation — and the Federal Reserve's response to it — will also be front and center this week. The October consumer price index is due out Tuesday morning, followed by the producer price index on Friday. As of Sunday, traders are pricing in 78% odds for a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool . Hot inflation data will likely prompt the market to price in additional tightening ahead, especially in light of an October jobs report on Friday that illustrated the resilience of the U.S. economy. In addition, a number of central bankers are set to give public remarks throughout the week, and their speeches carry market-moving potential of their own. Consider what happened in the runup to the Fed's October meeting, when New York Fed President John Williams said on Sept. 29 that he saw "no need for urgency" on another hike. The market had been pricing hikes at both the October and December meetings, but that shifted to just one additional hike after Williams' comments hit the tape. So, we need to pay attention to both the inflation reports and all the Fedspeak coming our way. Among them, we'll hear from Fed Governor Christopher Waller on Tuesday and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday. Both central bankers are voting members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year. items.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
items.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.
items.content:
By Daniel Bush ,Â  Washington correspondent Â  and Â  Madeline Halpert
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff , replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Image caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Image caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

How Big Oil Became the AI Industry's Favorite Customer
OpenAI, ADNOC and G42 signed a multi-year deal on Nov. 2 to put AI across the Abu Dhabi oil company's operations, the highest-profile example of tech firms pitching bespoke tools to oil clients at ADIPEC, Semafor reports.
The traffic runs both ways: Microsoft has a 20-year gas power deal with Chevron for a planned 2.67-gigawatt West Texas plant, and Amazon's planned Texas plant could become the country's biggest single emitter if built to its permit limits.
A peer-reviewed modeling study estimates that AI gains in fossil fuels would add 0.47 billion to 1.8 billion metric tons of CO2 a year even if renewables gain equally, with the low end comparable to Mexico's annual emissions, co-author Holly Alpine says.
Artificial intelligence companies are deepening their ties with the fossil fuel industries as some of the biggest names in the tech world make massive deals with energy companies, both to power their energy-hungry data centers and to embed machine learning into the energy sector itself. Already, the artificial intelligence boom is causing a natural gas surge in the United States, and experts expect that data center hyperscalers will greatly extend the life of fossil fuels in the global energy mix, even as the world continues to shatter clean energy growth records.
This Monday, OpenAI – the firm behind ChatGPT – made a deal with Abu Dhabi's ADNOC “to deploy advanced AI capabilities across the state energy firm's operations,” according to reporting from Reuters. The report noted that the agreement “mark[s] the latest step in the ChatGPT maker's deepening ties with the United Arab Emirates.”
But the trend extends far beyond just one firm and one country. Globally, AI firms are racing to make products designed for some of the richest pockets in the world – oil and gas companies. A recent report from nonpartisan global news outlet Semafor notes that the OpenAI-ADNOC deal “was the highest-profile example in a broader push at ADIPEC by tech companies to pitch bespoke, AI-driven tools to help operate drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets.”
What is more, the deepening ties between AI and fossil fuels goes both ways. Big Tech is planning data centers faster than global power grids can keep up. Plus, legislation under the Trump administration has pushed tech companies to provide their own energy sources to power new planned data centers, leaving Silicon Valley scrambling to add energy production capacity by any means necessary. While this includes funding research and development of next-gen clean energy technologies like nuclear fusion and space-based solar power, in practice it has translated to massive natural gas contracts.
At present, Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that, if completed according to the current plan involving the development of seven natural gas plants, will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States . In August, AI giant Nvidia announced that it would partner with Japan’s SoftBank and the United States federal government to build the largest fossil-fuel plant in the country in order to power an Ohio project by OpenAI. Microsoft, too, just signed a 20-year deal with Chevron to provide 2.67 gigawatts of natural-gas-fired power for a proposed West Texas data center.
AI advocates argue that in the long run, AI will save more energy than it consumes thanks to efficiency gains across all of the sectors that use it. However, those gains are a double-edged sword. A recent paper published by NPJ Climate Action found that, if fossil fuels make economic gains anywhere above zero thanks to AI integration, enabled emissions will exceed avoided emissions. In a scenario where both the fossil fuel and the renewables sector benefit equally from AI gains, global CO2 emissions will still increase by between 0.47 billion tons and 1.8 billion tons a year. “On the smaller side it's about the emissions of Mexico annually,” Holly Alpine, one of the co-authors of the research, was recently quoted by the Wall Street Journal.
Despite NPJ Climate Action’s sobering warning, AI firms are tripping over themselves to court fossil fuel companies and secure long-term contracts with economic heavyweights in Big Oil. The OpenAI-ADNOC deal is not the first of its kind, but the high-profile nature of the agreement is indicative of the direction that the sectors as a whole are heading – and it’s not good for anyone’s bottom line but their own.

items.summary: President Trump warns that US forces are 'locked and loaded' and ready to strike, if necessary.

Share Iran threatens to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war on social media
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued the 'rain down hell' warning on Sunday, November 8 [File: Vahid Salemi/AP]
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the United States resumes attacks, serving Washington with an ultimatum in an attempt to end the two countries’ eight-month war.
“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Araghchi wrote in a post on X on Sunday.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell,” he said.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran are “highly unlikely” if negotiations progress over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said when asked about continued US strikes on Iran during a phone interview reported by CNN. “I would [continue], if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” he added.
Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He also said that the US has 38 bridges in Iran’s crosshairs that US forces “can knock down in literally one hour”.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry also quoted Araghchi in an earlier statement on Sunday that said Iran would “not go easy on American targets” in the region.
Araghchi’s statements came after reports by state media that an oil tanker caught fire earlier that morning after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz , citing Iran’s navy.
The navy claimed the ship’s identification systems were turned off and it was travelling in the no-go zone of the strait.
An adviser to Iran’s commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Aerospace Force made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said that weapons have been “secured for years to come”.
“The armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe,” warned IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali in a statement on Telegram.
“As senior commanders of the armed forces have pointed out, we have upgraded our capabilities in the post-Ramadan War period,” Belali said.
The back-and-fourth between Iranian and US leaders comes following US midterm elections in which the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, soundly defeating Trump’s Republican Party.
Araghchi alleged that negotiations have been delayed as a result of the elections, but he awaits the path forward, Iranian state media reported.
“It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits,” the foreign minister said. “We have to wait.”

items.content:
SILVERDALE, Wash. — Members of the Central Kitsap Fire and Rescue (CKFR) report that they had a “unusual” Thursday morning last week.
According to CKFR on Facebook , their crews were sent to the 4600 block of NW Knute Anderson Road just after 9 a.m., Thursday, Nov. 5.
CKFR says a car went off the road and hit the corner of a nearby house, before stopping in that house’s backyard. During the crash, the person’s car hit the house’s natural gas meter, according to CKFR.
CKFR notes that they then had to work to stop any potential gas hazard. Puget Sound Energy and Cascade Natural Gas also showed up to the scene to help.
While there were people inside the house during the crash, CKFR clarifies that only the driver sustained minor injuries, and that they Kitsap County Sheriff’s Office is actively investigating the crash.
